qs.q: What is the primary site of productive infection for herpes simplex viruses?
qs.e: HSV replicates in mucosal epithelium at entry; latency is later established in sensory neurons. The other sites are not the main replication sites.

qs.q: In cases of Herpes simplex virus encephalitis, which region of the brain is classically and severely affected?
qs.e: In HSV encephalitis, the cerebral cortex, classically the temporal lobes in HSV-1 encephalitis, is often severely affected. Conversely, rabies has a predilection for the basal structures.

qs.q: Which medication is commonly used to treat esophageal ulcers associated with herpes simplex virus in HIV patients?
o: Nitazoxanide administered orally for parasitic infections
Azithromycin administered orally for bacterial pathogens
Fluconazole administered orally for fungal lesions
Acyclovir administered orally for mucosal ulcerations
qs.e: Esophageal ulcers associated with HSV are treated with acyclovir for 14 to 21 days, with foscarnet reserved for unresponsive cases. Fluconazole is used for fungal infections instead.

qs.q: A young adult presents with targetoid skin lesions featuring a pale vesicular center, following a recent herpes simplex virus infection. Which cells are primarily responsible for the direct tissue damage seen in this disorder?
o: Skin-homing cytotoxic T cells attacking basal cells of the skin and mucosae
CD4+ memory T cells releasing cytokines that induce intercellular epidermal oedema
Neutrophils accumulating beneath the stratum corneum to form subcorneal pustules
Mast cells releasing histamine and causing superficial dermal microvascular hyperpermeability
qs.e: Erythema multiforme is driven by skin-homing cytotoxic T cells that attack basal cells displaying cross-reacting antigens. Neutrophil accumulation beneath the stratum corneum is characteristic of impetigo.

qs.q: Which laboratory test finding from a Tzanck smear of a vesicular skin lesion is characteristic of both Herpes Simplex Virus and Varicella-Zoster Virus infections?
o: Multinucleated giant cells with inclusion bodies
Atypical Downey cells with indented nuclei
qs.e: Both HSV and VZV produce multinucleated giant cells and 'ground glass' chromatin on a Tzanck smear. Owl's eye intranuclear inclusions are characteristic of cytomegalovirus histology.
qs.s: Herpesviruses: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV, Symptoms, Diagnosis, Tx: MCQs

qs.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of acyclovir in the management of Herpes Simplex Virus and Varicella-Zoster Virus infections?
qs.e: Acyclovir acts by inhibiting viral DNA polymerase, thereby halting viral replication during active infection. It does not eliminate viral latency or prevent retrograde transport to ganglia.

qs.q: Which specific antiviral medication is used to treat herpes simplex virus‑related acute liver failure?
qs.e: Acyclovir is the targeted therapy for HSV infection. The other drugs treat different etiologies.

qs.q: What is the typical microscopic finding in a Tzanck smear of vesicular fluid taken from a patient with a herpes simplex lesion?
qs.e: A Tzanck smear typically shows multinucleated giant cells with 'ground glass' chromatin for both HSV and VZV. Owl's eye inclusions are characteristic of cytomegalovirus histology.

es.q: Herpesviridae are significant human pathogens known for their ability to establish latency and cause recurrent disease. 1. Briefly describe the general characteristics of all Herpesviruses. (3 marks) 2. Compare and contrast the pathogenesis, typical clinical presentations, and common latency sites f

ai.title: Herpes Simplex Virus Infection
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) causes mucocutaneous lesions, encephalitis and neonatal disease. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and targeted tests, while management balances antiviral therapy with supportive care, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: HSV infection is a viral disease caused by HSV‑1 or HSV‑2. It presents as recurrent mucocutaneous ulcers, neonatal disease, or encephalitis. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by PCR or viral culture when available.
b: Typical vesicular lesions on lips (HSV‑1) or genitalia (HSV‑2)
Fever, headache, altered mental status suggest encephalitis

t.a: PCR of lesion swab or CSF
t.b: Confirms HSV type and guides antiviral choice; positive = start acyclovir, negative = consider other etiologies
Shows multinucleated giant cells; supportive but not type‑specific
Detects recent infection; limited utility in acute setting

sections.p: Severity is judged by lesion extent, systemic involvement and host factors (e.g., HIV, pregnancy). Encephalitis is stage 4 (life‑threatening).
b: Mild: localized oral/genital lesions
Moderate: extensive lesions, systemic symptoms
Severe: encephalitis, neonatal disease, disseminated infection

sections.p: HSV is acquired through direct contact with infected secretions. In East Africa, HSV‑2 genital infection is common, often co‑existing with other ulcerative STIs.
b: Sexual contact (heterosexual intercourse)
Perinatal transmission (neonatal HSV)
Contact with oral lesions (cold sores)
Reactivation from latency in sensory ganglia

sections.p: Presentation varies by site and host immunity.
b: Oral HSV‑1: grouped vesicles on erythematous base, crusting after 7‑10 days
Genital HSV‑2: painful vesicles → ulceration, tender inguinal nodes
Neonatal HSV: vesicular rash, fever, seizures, organ failure
HSV encephalitis: fever, headache, seizures, focal deficits, rapid deterioration

sections.p: Select tests that answer the clinical question; when unavailable, treat empirically.

t.b: Confirms encephalitis; positive → start IV acyclovir, negative → look for other causes
Identifies HSV type; guides oral antiviral choice
Detects secondary infection, dehydration; guides supportive care

t.a: If PCR unavailable, start empirical acyclovir for suspected encephalitis

sections.p: Complications are more common in immunocompromised or neonates.
b: Encephalitis – high mortality without antivirals
Disseminated neonatal disease – organ failure
Secondary bacterial infection of lesions
Herpetic keratitis – vision loss

sections.p: Treat active infection, prevent recurrence and address complications.
b: Oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir for mucocutaneous disease
Pain control with NSAIDs; avoid topical steroids on active lesions
In HIV patients, ensure ART adherence to reduce reactivation

sections.p: Monitor for healing, recurrence and drug toxicity; counsel on transmission reduction.
b: Review lesion healing in 7‑10 days; if no improvement, reassess diagnosis
Educate on condom use, avoiding contact during active lesions
Suppressive therapy (e.g., daily oral antiviral) for frequent recurrences or pregnant women
Screen sexual partners and provide counseling

sections.p: Other ulcerating infections can mimic HSV lesions.
b: Syphilis chancre – painless, single ulcer
Chancroid – painful, ragged ulcer with tender nodes
Varicella‑zoster – dermatomal distribution, usually unilateral
Aphthous ulcer – non‑vesicular, no viral prodrome

sections.p: Laboratory findings may be falsely reassuring.
b: Negative Tzanck smear does not rule out HSV
Serology may be positive from past infection, not active disease
CSF PCR can be negative early; repeat if suspicion remains

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening mental status or seizures (possible encephalitis)
Neonatal vesicular rash with fever or seizures
Severe pain, spreading ulceration, or signs of secondary bacterial infection

faq.a: No; antivirals suppress replication but the virus remains latent.

faq.q: Is HSV‑1 only oral and HSV‑2 only genital?
faq.a: Primarily, but both types can infect either site.
For ≥4 recurrences per year, genital infection in pregnancy, or immunocompromised patients.
